title: CHAPTER 23: ECONOMIC REFORMS IN INDIA (1991 – LPG MODEL)

blocks.content: INTRODUCTION TO ECONOMIC REFORMS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The 1991 Economic Reforms were introduced to handle a critical Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis and severe foreign exchange depletion.
Liberalisation dismantled the bureaucratic 'License-Permit Raj' and reduced state control over economic activities.
Privatisation aimed at improving efficiency in public sector enterprises via disinvestment and private participation.
Globalisation integrated the Indian economy with global trade by rationalizing tariffs and encouraging Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
The New Industrial Policy of 1991 substantially reduced the number of sectors reserved exclusively for the public domain.

BACKGROUND OF ECONOMIC REFORMS (WHY 1991 REFORMS WERE NEEDED)
By 1990–91, India faced a severe economic crisis due to:
India had very low foreign exchange reserves (only enough for 2 weeks of imports).
Government expenditure was very high compared to income.
Prices of essential goods were rising rapidly.
Industries were inefficient due to government control.
India had borrowed heavily from foreign countries.
Oil prices increased and remittances decreased.
Due to these reasons, India had no option but to reform its economy.
ROLE OF IMF AND WORLD BANK

The LPG Model of 1991 marked a structural shift in the Indian economy from a socialist planning model to a market-driven economy.
LPG MODEL OF ECONOMIC REFORMS
Economic Reforms of 1991 are based on three major pillars:
L – Liberalisation P – Privatisation G – Globalisation
Together, they are called LPG Reforms.

CONCLUSION

Economic Reforms of 1991 changed the face of Indian economy. They helped India move from a closed economy to a global economy. Though challenges exist, LPG reforms have played a major role in making India one of the fastest growing economies in the world.
